Since then, more than 10,000 of them have made their way to people around the world. While building Reachy Mini, we kept coming back to another question: what would a small robot look like if its main job was not to stay on a desk and interact with you, but to move through the world? Microduck came out of that question. Microduck is a 25 cm tall biped robot with 15 motors, a camera, a small depth sensor, two IMUs, and an articulated beak that can pick up objects. It can walk, sit, crouch, get back up from many common falls, and even roller-skate. og_title: SLAM on Microduck with an 8×8 depth sensor
og_desc: Microduck maps the room it walks in and finds itself again after being carried somewhere else, with leg odometry and an 8×8 depth sensor, fully onboard. How it works, and how a ground-truth rig turned a map that looked like noise into one we can measure.
text_start: SLAM on Microduck with an 8×8 depth sensor | Pollen Robotics Pollen Robotics × Hugging Face Pollen Reachy Mini Microduck Reachy 2 Microduck Blog Press kit Simulator Pre-order Microduck › Blog › SLAM on Microduck with an 8×8 depth sensor Engineering SLAM on Microduck with an 8×8 depth sensor Antoine Pirrone October 23, 2026 · 15 min read The odometry post ended on a promise. Odometry tells you how the duck has moved since it booted. It is good, but it drifts. On the real robot we measured it over 47.5 m of walking, cut into twenty walks of half a metre to five metres. At the end of a walk it was 6 cm off on median, and 12 cm at worst: about 2.4 cm of error for every metre walked. Its heading also ended about 2° off, and that matters more than it sounds. With a 2° error, every metre walked afterwards puts the duck 3.5 cm to the side of where odometry thinks it is. So the longer the duck walks, the further its estimate drifts from the truth. After a few minutes of play, it has little to do with the room. It gets worse when somebody picks the duck up, because odometry cannot feel it.
